ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Gauging, Philadelphia, PA
ut.description: UT inspection in Philadelphia, PA: thickness surveys on terminal tanks, process piping and steel bridge members, plus shear wave weld work. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Philadelphia terminals, plants, shipyards and structures for ultrasonic thickness testing and shear wave weld examination. Typical jobs are corrosion surveys on tanks and process piping along the Delaware River, section-loss checks on steel members, and weld examination on pressure piping and fabrications. A written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III controls the work. Send your scope through this UT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Philadelphia

Philadelphia has been an industrial port city for more than two centuries, and that history shows in the steel that still needs inspection. South Philadelphia was home to a large refinery complex until a 2019 fire ended its operation; the site is now being redeveloped as the Bellwether District for logistics, e-commerce and life sciences, while petroleum and chemical storage and terminal operations continue along the Delaware River. Elsewhere in the city, the inspection demand is varied and steady.

  • Aboveground storage tank shells, nozzles and attached piping at river terminals.
  • Process, steam, condensate and chilled water piping at pharmaceutical, life sciences and food plants.
  • Natural gas distribution and storage facilities, including pressure piping and regulator stations.
  • Hull plate and tank boundaries on vessels at the Navy Yard shipyard and on port-call ships.
  • Steel members on bridges, viaducts, rail structures and port cranes, where section loss from decades of weather has to be measured.
  • Pressure vessels and boilers in hospitals, universities and district energy plants.

Thickness surveys on Philadelphia piping, tanks and structures

Thickness testing answers how much steel remains at the points that matter. On piping and vessels the technician reads at agreed condition monitoring locations using a dual-element probe, calibrated on a step block of matching material, with the A-scan watched so doubling or lamination is recognized. High-temperature probes and couplant handle hot steam and process lines, with a velocity correction for temperature. The method is described in ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797); our plain-language guide is ultrasonic thickness measurement requirements.

Structures need a different mindset. On a bridge or crane the technician reads the web, flange or gusset at marked sections, and the surface may be heavily layered with paint and rust. The owner decides how much coating to strip, and the report distinguishes between readings through sound paint and readings at bare metal. In Philadelphia's humid air, corrosion under pack rust, at drainage points and beneath deck joints is a common finding.

Shear wave weld examination in Philadelphia

For weld volume, the technician uses an angle-beam probe, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees, calibrated against a reference level or distance-amplitude curve built from side-drilled holes. The weld is scanned from both sides where geometry allows, indications are plotted, and each is evaluated against the construction code's table. Lack of fusion, cracks and slag are the typical targets.

The procedure traces to ASME Section V Article 4, and the acceptance rules come from the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.6 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 Clause 8 for structural steel, or AWS D1.5 for highway bridges. Using UT in place of radiography is a decision made in the specification before the work begins; see our national ultrasonic testing service for scope detail.

Limits of ultrasonic testing

No method sees everything. Ultrasound loses strength in coarse-grained cast stainless and in austenitic welds, where the beam scatters. Heavy corrosion pitting and rough scale can break couplant contact, and a probe cannot read through a thick, poorly bonded coating. Flaws parallel to the beam may be missed, and the dead zone just under the probe makes very thin or surface-breaking flaws hard to separate from the front echo.

Because of these limits, Philadelphia scopes often pair UT with another method. A bridge weld may get UT for the volume and magnetic particle testing for the toe, while stainless pharmaceutical piping may rely on liquid penetrant testing for surface cracks. The report states what was examined and what was not.

Codes and the Pennsylvania boiler regime

Owner programs for refining and terminal assets lean on API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks, and under each of them the owner's authorized inspector carries responsibility for the inspection. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports thickness and flaw data. OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), expects mechanical integrity inspection to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 cover gas and liquid pipelines.

Pennsylvania regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels through the Department of Labor and Industry's Boiler Division. A commissioned inspector, holding a Pennsylvania commission backed by a National Board commission, performs the inspection, and the division issues a Certificate of Operation; the state lists 36 months for unfired pressure vessels, with internal examination possible on age or condition. The Pennsylvania boiler and unfired pressure vessel page describes the system. Our thickness and weld data goes to whoever signs the record.

Preparing the component and the access

An ultrasonic probe needs a repeatable contact surface. For thickness work the owner removes loose scale and flaking paint at each marked location, and where insulation is present, windows are cut or lagging is pulled so the probe reaches steel. For weld scans, a clean strip beside the weld is needed wide enough for the probe to travel back and forth, and the weld cap may need dressing if its shape blocks coupling.

Before work, send isometrics, vessel drawings, any prior survey data and a note about known damage mechanisms. On Philadelphia structures that note may be about deck drainage and pack rust; at a terminal it might be bottom-side corrosion, soil contact at tank chimes, or product service. Access is part of preparation too: scaffolding, lifts, confined-space permits, fall protection and a place to set the instrument down safely.

Corrosion mechanisms Philadelphia owners track

Most thickness programs in the city follow a few mechanisms. Atmospheric and under-insulation corrosion affect piping and vessels exposed to humid air, and the pockets where water collects at supports, clamps and low points are the first to go. In terminals, tank shells and bottom-edge areas see wet and dry cycling, and nozzle necks and attached piping thin at points of turbulence. In steam and condensate systems, erosion and flow-accelerated corrosion thin elbows and downstream pipe, even though the metal looks sound outside.

On steel structures the pattern is different: section loss at joints, bearings and drainage points where water and salt sit. Ultrasonic thickness readings on those members tell the owner's engineer how much cross-section remains and whether the loss is local or general, which is the input for a load rating or repair design.

A sample UT scope for a Philadelphia terminal

A typical enquiry reads: a river terminal wants shell thickness readings on a product tank before a scheduled out-of-service inspection, together with readings on the nozzle necks and the first elbows of the attached piping. The scope gives the tank's course heights and plate thickness, the grid spacing, the surface condition and the code. Our technician marks a grid, records readings with a dual-element probe, flags any area below the minimum, and delivers a table the owner's authorized inspector can use to calculate remaining life.

Steam, condensate and utility piping

Hospitals, universities and district energy plants in Philadelphia run steam and condensate lines that were installed long ago and keep thinning at the same places: elbows, reducers, drip legs and low points where condensate collects. Thickness testing at marked locations shows how fast wall is disappearing, and it can be done on hot lines with high-temperature probes and couplant.

The owner usually supplies pipe schedules and prior readings, and the technician repeats the same locations each time so the corrosion rate is a real trend, not a coincidence of probe placement. Where a line is insulated, small windows are cut and resealed by the owner's insulator after the readings are taken.

Who performs the work

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, an employer-based system. A Level II calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets results. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports; that role is held by founder Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Owners who want their own program reviewed can use written practice development or Level III consulting.

What the UT report contains

  • Component, weld or structure ID, drawing or isometric reference, and the acceptance code.
  • Procedure ID and revision, with the probe, frequency, wedge angle and couplant that were used.
  • Instrument and calibration block, calibration checks and surface temperature.
  • Technician name and level, with the reviewing Level III.
  • For welds, each reflector with position, length and amplitude and an accept or reject call; for thickness work, a location table or grid showing nominal wall, measured wall and the trend against earlier surveys.
  • Areas not examined and the reason, such as access, coating or insulation.

Planning a UT job in Philadelphia

The city has humid summers and cold winters with freeze and thaw cycles, plus rain and fog off the rivers. Couplant selection, instrument protection and surface moisture all depend on the season. Outdoor structure work on bridges and rail corridors usually needs traffic or track access arranged by the owner, which can make scheduling the longest lead item. Port terminals have their own security and credential requirements.

Atlantis keeps no office in Philadelphia. Technicians travel to your terminal, plant or structure from outside the area, so plan for badging, safety orientation, confined-space permits, fall protection and access equipment on the owner's side. Share line sizes, insulation, temperature and code with the request and the quote will match the real work.

Ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant testing in Philadelphia

Choose ultrasonic testing for wall thickness and internal weld flaws. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Philadelphia for surface cracks in carbon steel welds and structural details, and liquid penetrant testing in Philadelphia for stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. The ultrasonic testing guide gives a plain-language overview, and the state hub at NDT inspection services in Pennsylvania lists wider coverage.

Training your own UT technicians

Companies in Philadelphia that want their own ultrasonic capability can start with UT Level 1 training or UT Level 2 training, rehearse on the UT practical simulator, and see NDT training for Philadelphia for delivery options. Employers certify under their own written practice.

faq.q: What kinds of sites does UT cover in Philadelphia?
faq.a: Terminal tanks and piping on the Delaware River, process and utility piping at pharmaceutical and food plants, gas facilities, vessels at the Navy Yard, and steel on bridges, rail structures and port cranes.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic thickness testing be done through paint on a bridge?
faq.a: Sometimes. If the coating is thin and well bonded, a procedure checked against it can work, but heavy or flaking layers must be removed. The report records whether each reading was taken through coating or on bare metal.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Philadelphia?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city for the agreed scope, so travel, access and credentials for terminals or structures are planned when you request the quote.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on Philadelphia welds?
faq.a: Where ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 or Section VIII allow it, and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree beforehand. The substitution should be written into the specification, not decided during the job.

faq.q: Which codes govern the UT work?
faq.a: The examination procedure follows ASME Section V Articles 4, 5 or 23, and acceptance comes from ASME Section VIII, B31.3, API 510, 570 or 653, AWS D1.1 or D1.5, depending on the item and the owner.

faq.q: Who inspects boilers and pressure vessels in Pennsylvania?
faq.a: Inspectors who hold a Pennsylvania commission, backed by a National Board commission, perform the inspections, and the Department of Labor and Industry Boiler Division issues the Certificate of Operation. The owner's insurer or the Commonwealth may supply the inspector.

faq.q: What reduces the quality of ultrasonic results?
faq.a: Rough or pitted surfaces, thick or loose coatings, coarse-grained material, hot surfaces without suitable probes, and flaws aligned with the beam. The technician records limitations in the report.

faq.q: How are thickness readings repeated between surveys?
faq.a: Each location has an ID and a marked position on a drawing or the component, and the technician returns to the same point with the same probe type and calibration approach so the corrosion trend is comparable.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train our inspectors in UT?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A and a browser-based simulator. Your company certifies its personnel under its own written practice.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Philadelphia, PA
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Philadelphia, PA for steel bridges, port cranes, tank and piping welds and fabrications, by yoke or wet method. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT travels to Philadelphia sites to perform magnetic particle inspection on carbon and low-alloy steel: bridge and viaduct welds, port crane structures, tank and piping welds, railcar and heavy fabrication. Technicians work to a procedure written to ASME Section V Article 7 or the owner's specification, and every indication is located, measured and called accept or reject against the named criteria. Request a MT inspection quote for Philadelphia and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Philadelphia

Philadelphia carries more steel across water than most cities its size. The Delaware and Schuylkill crossings, elevated highways, rail bridges and the container terminals on the river all depend on welded and bolted carbon steel that sees fatigue every day. Add the shipyard at the Navy Yard, tank terminals, and a long list of fabrication and machine shops, and magnetic particle inspection has plenty to do.

  • Weld toes, cover plates, stiffener ends and repair welds on steel bridge girders and floor beams.
  • Gantry crane structures, spreader components and lifting lugs at port terminals.
  • Tank shell-to-bottom and nozzle welds, and carbon steel process piping repairs.
  • Railcar, rail yard and locomotive repair welds and heavy rolling-stock components.
  • Shipboard foundations, hull-attached fittings and lifting padeyes during ship repair.
  • Fabrication shop acceptance of structural and mechanical assemblies.

What MT finds, and where it stops

The method magnetizes the part and applies fine ferromagnetic particles that cluster where a crack or similar discontinuity leaks flux. It detects surface-breaking cracks and flaws just beneath the surface, such as lack of fusion at a weld toe or a fatigue crack growing from a bolt hole. It cannot be used on non-magnetic metals, so the austenitic stainless piping common in Philadelphia's pharmaceutical and food plants needs liquid penetrant testing instead.

Direction also matters. A crack parallel to the magnetic field produces almost no leakage, which is why ASME Section V requires two examinations with the field at roughly right angles. Paint, rust and weld spatter dampen sensitivity, and anything buried deeper than a fraction of an inch is out of range. The answer to what is inside the weld comes from ultrasonic testing in Philadelphia.

Techniques used on Philadelphia jobs

For field work the tool of choice is an electromagnetic yoke with adjustable legs. ASME Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds (4.5 kg) at the maximum pole spacing, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds (18 kg), so the technician verifies lifting power with a test weight. Prods can push current through a thicker section but risk arc burns, and many owners, including highway agencies, restrict them on finished steel.

Particles come as dry powder for hot, rough or outdoor surfaces and as a wet suspension for greater sensitivity. Wet visible particles over a thin white contrast coating work well on bridge and crane steel in daylight. Fluorescent particles need UV-A light and a darkened enclosure, which technicians build with shrouds or work inside tank and hull spaces. Parts that will be welded, machined or placed near sensitive equipment are demagnetized and checked for residual field.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply in Philadelphia

The method standard is ASME Section V Article 7, supported by ASTM E1444 and ASTM E709. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and AWS D1.5 where the owner is a highway agency or authority and the work is steel bridge welding. Under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector accepts repairs and uses our indication data for the record.

Pennsylvania's Department of Labor and Industry Boiler Division regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels, and welded repairs on them must be made by a repair organization holding a National Board R stamp with a commissioned inspector involved. For a plain-language reading of the method, see Article 7 requirements explained.

Fatigue cracking on Philadelphia's older steel

Much of the steel around Philadelphia was built decades ago for lighter traffic and fewer load cycles than it carries today. Fatigue cracks tend to start at details rather than in the open plate: the end of a cover plate, a welded attachment, a bolt hole or a repair weld whose toe was left sharp. A crack at a detail like that may be only a few millimeters long when it first appears, and magnetic particle inspection is one of the most practical ways to find it before it becomes a fracture.

Because the surface is usually painted, the technician works with the owner on how much coating to remove. Typically a window is opened at each detail, the steel is cleaned to bare metal, and the area is examined and then recoated by the owner's painter. Where a crack is confirmed, the owner's engineer decides on a repair, such as drilling a stop hole or weld repair, and a follow-up examination confirms the work.

Surface preparation and contrast

Particles can only gather where the surface is clean enough for them to move. Heavy rust, oil, grease and mill scale are removed with wire brushes, flap discs or solvent, and the cleaned area extends beyond the weld by enough margin to show the heat-affected zone. A thin white contrast coating is applied for visible wet work, so a dark particle line is easy to see and photograph against it.

On bridges and port structures the real limitation is access rather than cleaning. Technicians may work from an under-bridge inspection vehicle, a lift or rope-supported platforms arranged by the owner, and cannot always reach every detail from a safe working position. The report lists details that were not reachable so the owner knows what remains.

Typical findings and how they are handled

MT indications on Philadelphia jobs fall into a short list: linear crack-like lines at weld toes, lack of fusion at sidewalls, laps and seams in rolled shapes, arc strikes, and the marks left by aggressive grinding. A relevant indication is measured, and the acceptance table of the governing code decides what it means. For many codes any linear crack-like indication is rejected regardless of length, while rounded indications may be allowed up to a stated size.

The usual repair path is to grind out the indication, re-examine the ground area with magnetic particles, and weld only when the crack is gone. If grinding removes more metal than the repair procedure allows, an ultrasonic thickness reading is taken to confirm the remaining section. Each step is written into the report, so the owner holds one continuous record from discovery to closure.

A sample MT scope for a Philadelphia structure

A typical request might read: a steel bridge's floor beams have shown cracking at the ends of welded cover plates, and the owner wants the cover plate ends and adjacent welds on eight beams examined by magnetic particles with a yoke, after paint removal at each location. The scope names the specification, acceptance criteria, access method, and traffic restrictions. Our technician examines each detail in two perpendicular directions, records every indication on sketches, and delivers a report that the owner's engineer can attach to the repair design.

Port cranes and the container terminals

Container and bulk terminals on the Delaware River depend on gantry cranes, straddle carriers, spreaders and rail-mounted equipment, all of which flex thousands of times a day. Welded boom joints, sill beam connections, trolley rails and spreader twist-lock housings are watched closely because a failure stops a berth. Magnetic particle inspection is the usual check on those welds during planned maintenance, and it can be done on a lifted or lowered boom with a yoke and portable lighting.

Access to terminals is controlled, so technicians present credentials, attend site safety orientation and work around vessel schedules. The owner's maintenance planner usually arranges the crane outage, lockout and fall protection, and the technician examines the welds listed on the work order and reports each by its position on the boom drawing.

On structures, the inspection record usually becomes part of a larger condition file, so each examined detail is tied to a drawing location, a girder line and a span. That discipline pays off the next time the owner returns to the same detail and wants to know whether an indication has grown.

Who performs MT and how it is reviewed

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, where the employer is the certifying body. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications. An ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews reports. If your own program needs a procedure or written practice, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

What the MT report contains

  • Component, weld or structure ID, drawing reference, material and governing code.
  • Procedure ID and revision, the magnetizing technique (yoke, prods or coil), the current type and the particle type.
  • Yoke lift check, UV-A and ambient light readings for fluorescent work, and equipment identification.
  • Technician name and level, with the reviewing Level III.
  • Each indication with location, length and orientation, supported by sketch or photograph, and the accept or reject decision.
  • Demagnetization result where the specification calls for it.

Planning an MT job in Philadelphia

Humidity is the usual enemy. Along the rivers, dew forms on steel during the night and in the early morning, and moisture changes how wet particles and contrast coatings behave. Winter cold slows drying and can thicken wet carriers, while summer heat can dry them too quickly. The surface temperature goes into the report because the procedure covers a stated range.

Atlantis keeps no office in Philadelphia. Technicians come to your site with their own yokes, lights and test blocks, so allow for port credentials, rail or road closures for structures, hot-work and confined-space permits, and access equipment. Tell us the dates early, especially if the work depends on a traffic window or a ship's repair schedule.

MT, PT or UT for your Philadelphia job

Pick MT for carbon steel welds and fatigue-critical details, PT for stainless steel and non-magnetic metals, and UT for thickness and internal flaws. The MT versus PT comparison helps you pick, the magnetic particle testing guide explains the method end to end, and NDT inspection services in Pennsylvania covers the wider state.

Training your own MT technicians

Teams in Philadelphia that want to run their own examinations can begin with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and see NDT training for Philadelphia for delivery details. Employers certify under their own written practice.

faq.q: What steel structures in Philadelphia are examined with MT?
faq.a: Bridge girders and floor beams, port cranes, rail structures, tank and piping welds, railcar repairs, ship repair fittings and shop fabrications. The method suits carbon and low-alloy steel with accessible weld surfaces.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel piping at a pharmaceutical plant?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, which is not magnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is used on those materials to find surface-breaking flaws, and ultrasonic testing covers thickness and internal weld flaws.

faq.q: Does Atlantis maintain a Philadelphia crew?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your site for the agreed scope, so travel, credentials and access are planned and included in the quote.

faq.q: Are prods acceptable on bridge steel?
faq.a: Often not. Prods can cause arc burns, so many highway agencies and owners restrict or prohibit them on finished surfaces. A yoke is normally specified, and the procedure states what is allowed.

faq.q: How does humidity affect magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Dew and moisture alter how particles flow and how contrast coatings dry. The technician wipes the surface dry, controls the carrier and records surface temperature, and may shift work to the part of the day when conditions suit the procedure.

faq.q: What does AWS D1.5 mean for MT work?
faq.a: AWS D1.5 is the Bridge Welding Code used by many highway agencies. It sets acceptance criteria for welds on steel bridges, and MT procedures for such work must follow the owner's specification and the applicable edition.

faq.q: Who accepts repairs on pressure vessels in Pennsylvania?
faq.a: The authorized inspector or commissioned inspector responsible for the equipment. Pennsylvania's Department of Labor and Industry Boiler Division regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels, and welded repairs require a National Board R stamp holder.

faq.q: When is demagnetization required?
faq.a: When residual magnetism could affect later welding, machining, instruments or moving parts. The technician measures the residual field with a gauge or indicator and records the result in the report.

faq.q: Can my team learn MT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A, with practice tests, and your employer certifies personnel under its own written practice.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Philadelphia, PA
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in Philadelphia, PA for stainless pharma piping, aluminum, nickel alloys, castings and weld repairs. Send your parts for a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Philadelphia plants, shops and terminals for liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection, on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, castings and weld repairs. The method finds flaws that are open to the surface and works on metals that magnetic particle testing cannot examine. The procedure follows ASME Section V Article 6 or the owner's own specification. Describe the parts through this PT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Philadelphia

Philadelphia has one of the densest life sciences and pharmaceutical clusters on the East Coast, and those plants run on stainless steel: vessels, process piping and utility lines whose welds must be checked for surface cracks without introducing contaminants. The city also has food and beverage producers, chemical and consumer-products manufacturing, port equipment, shipyard work and a deep base of machine shops handling aluminum and alloy parts. In every one of them, penetrant is the practical surface method for non-magnetic material.

  • Austenitic stainless process and utility piping welds, vessel nozzle welds and repair areas.
  • Heat exchanger tubesheet welds and shell repairs at plants and district energy facilities.
  • Aluminum and nickel alloy fabrications, castings and forgings from machine shops.
  • Weld repairs on carbon steel where the owner wants penetrant to confirm a crack indication.
  • Shipboard stainless and non-ferrous fittings during ship repair at the river yards.

What penetrant finds, and what it cannot

PT detects discontinuities that are open to the surface. Capillary action draws a thin liquid into cracks, laps and surface porosity; after excess is removed, developer draws the liquid back out and the flaw shows as a visible mark. It works on any non-porous metal, which is why it is the surface check of choice for stainless steel, aluminum and titanium.

It will not show anything closed to the surface, and smearing from grinding, wire brushing or machining can seal a crack so that penetrant cannot enter. Porous surfaces absorb liquid and create misleading background. Internal weld flaws and wall loss need ultrasonic testing in Philadelphia, and fatigue cracks in carbon steel welds are often examined faster with magnetic particle inspection.

Technique, step by step

Every penetrant job follows the same order. The surface is cleaned and dried, penetrant is applied and left to dwell, the excess is removed, developer is applied, and the area is evaluated after a development time. In Philadelphia the field standard is a solvent-removable visible system, because it needs no running water or darkened room, and it can be used on stainless piping inside a plant without wetting the area. Fluorescent systems, evaluated with UV-A light in darkness, are chosen where greater sensitivity is required, such as critical stainless welds and aluminum castings.

Dwell and development times are taken from the procedure, not from the can. Wiping too aggressively can pull penetrant from a shallow crack, while too much developer can mask a fine indication. After evaluation, residues are removed so they do not affect later welding, cleaning validation or service fluids.

Temperature, humidity and contamination control in Philadelphia

ASME Section V Article 6 gives a standard temperature range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit (5 to 52 degrees Celsius) for the part and penetrant materials. Philadelphia winters push outdoor steel below that range, and sun-heated steel in summer can exceed it, so surface temperature is measured and recorded, and warming or shading is used when necessary. Humid air and dew can leave a film on a cleaned surface, so cleaning and application are done in sequence without long gaps.

Pharmaceutical and food plants add contamination rules of their own. For nickel alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium, penetrant materials are controlled for halogen and sulfur content and traceable by lot, and owners often require full post-cleaning with documentation so no residue stays in clean service. Technicians coordinate those requirements with the owner's quality unit before work begins.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The method standard is ASME Section V Article 6, supported by ASTM E165 for general industry. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural welds. Crack-like linear indications are generally rejected, and rounded indications are measured against a stated size limit.

Pennsylvania's Department of Labor and Industry Boiler Division regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels, and welded repairs must be made by a National Board R stamp holder with a commissioned inspector involved. Under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector accepts repairs; our report gives that inspector the data. See Article 6 requirements explained for a plain-language walk-through.

Surface preparation and when etching is needed

Penetrant has to enter the flaw, so the surface must be open and clean. Oil, paint, rust and process residue are removed first, usually with a solvent cleaner and lint-free wipes, and the part is allowed to dry fully so no cleaner remains in a crack. On new stainless welds the technician often finds a light oxide tint, which is removed or accepted according to the owner's cleanliness standard before testing.

Where grinding, wire brushing, shot blasting or machining has smeared metal across the surface, cracks can be sealed. In those cases the procedure calls for chemical etching or fine mechanical conditioning to reopen the surface, followed by neutralizing and drying. Etching on a pharmaceutical system must be done under the owner's controls and with proper rinse verification, so we plan the sequence with their quality staff before work begins.

Visible or fluorescent penetrant

Visible penetrant is red dye on a white developer background and can be evaluated in normal light. It is quick to deploy, tolerates outdoor conditions and is the usual choice for field weld checks. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light and gives higher sensitivity for fine tight cracks, which suits critical stainless welds, aluminum castings and machined parts. It needs a darkened area and a calibrated UV-A source, so it is more often used in a shop than on a structure.

The choice follows the procedure and the owner's specification. Switching methods mid-job, or from one penetrant family to another, can be an issue because penetrant materials must be compatible within a system; mixing brands is not allowed unless the procedure says it is.

Typical findings and how they are handled

Penetrant indications on Philadelphia stainless and aluminum work include weld crater cracks, toe cracks, porosity breaking the surface, laps in forged fittings and tool marks mistaken for cracks. A relevant indication is measured and compared with the acceptance table, and doubtful ones are cleaned and retested rather than guessed. Many owners require a retest after a repair, and that follow-up is logged against the original indication number.

When a crack is confirmed in stainless steel it is ground out and the area is re-examined before welding. After welding, the repaired weld is retested and the surrounding area cleaned again. The report keeps the whole sequence so an auditor can follow it.

A sample PT scope for a Philadelphia pharmaceutical plant

A typical enquiry reads like this: a stainless steel process vessel at a life sciences facility received new nozzle welds during a shutdown, and the owner wants liquid penetrant testing of the nozzle-to-shell welds and repair areas, with documented post-cleaning. The scope states the procedure, the acceptance criteria, the cleanliness requirements and the location of the vessel. Our technician uses lot-certified, low-halogen materials, evaluates each weld, records indications, and returns a report that the quality unit can file with the change record.

Aluminum, alloy parts and shipyard work

Aluminum and nickel alloy work cannot be checked with magnetic particles, so penetrant carries the load. Philadelphia machine shops weld aluminum frames and marine parts, and the Navy Yard shipyard handles hull fittings, piping and non-ferrous components where surface cracks matter. Aluminum is soft, which makes smeared metal a particular concern after grinding or machining, and its thin oxide film means the cleaner and penetrant must be chosen to suit the alloy.

On ship repair jobs the schedule is tight and the space is cramped. Technicians work inside tanks, void spaces and machinery compartments with portable lighting, and ventilation, gas-free certificates and standby personnel are arranged by the yard before entry.

Who performs penetrant testing

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which the employer is the certifying body. A Level II performs the test and evaluates indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. For help writing a penetrant procedure or reviewing a written practice, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

What the PT report contains

  • Identification of the weld or part, its material, the drawing it comes from and the code in force.
  • Procedure number and revision, penetrant type and method, developer and the lot numbers used.
  • Surface temperature, dwell time and development time.
  • Technician name and level, with the reviewing Level III.
  • Each indication with location, size and photograph or sketch, and the accept or reject decision.
  • Post-cleaning confirmation for clean-service systems.

Planning a PT job in Philadelphia

Atlantis keeps no office in Philadelphia. Technicians travel to your plant, shop or terminal with their consumables, lights and test blocks, so tell us the material, surface condition, temperature and cleanliness requirements when you request the quote. Pharmaceutical suites, food plants and port terminals each have gowning, credential or safety requirements that need to be arranged before the technician travels.

If the area is large, expect it to be worked in sections so that no cleaned surface sits long enough to pick up moisture or dust. Share the shutdown or outage dates early, since PT is normally scheduled after welding and grinding and before painting or passivation.

Document requirements deserve a mention too. Life sciences owners often want lot numbers, certificates of analysis for penetrant materials and signed cleaning records filed with the work order, so ask your quality group what they need and share it with the quote request. That avoids a second visit just to complete paperwork.

PT, MT or UT for your Philadelphia job

Use PT for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any non-magnetic surface. Use MT on carbon steel welds when speed and toe sensitivity matter, and UT for thickness and internal flaws. The MT versus PT comparison helps decide, our national penetrant testing service lists standard scope, and NDT inspection services in Pennsylvania covers the wider state.

Training your own PT technicians

Teams that want their own penetrant capability can begin with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, practice on the penetrant testing simulator, and see NDT training for Philadelphia for delivery details. Your employer certifies personnel under its own written practice.

faq.q: Why is penetrant testing common at Philadelphia pharmaceutical plants?
faq.a: Pharmaceutical process piping and vessels are largely austenitic stainless steel, which cannot be examined by magnetic particle testing. Penetrant reveals surface-breaking cracks on welds and fittings without a magnetic field.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and penetrant materials. Colder or hotter work needs a procedure qualified for the temperature actually found at the weld.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Philadelphia office for PT?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your plant, shop or terminal, with travel, access and gowning or credential requirements agreed during quoting.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing leave residues in clean service systems?
faq.a: It can, which is why post-cleaning is part of the procedure for clean-service equipment. The technician follows the owner's cleaning requirements and documents residue removal in the report.

faq.q: How do I know if PT or MT is right for my weld?
faq.a: If the metal is magnetic carbon steel, MT is usually faster and finds near-surface flaws too. If it is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic metal, PT is the choice. Both only show surface-related flaws.

faq.q: Which standards cover PT of welds?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 for the method, with acceptance from ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 or AWS D1.1, as the work requires. ASTM E165 supports general industry practice.

faq.q: Who approves repairs on pressure vessels in Pennsylvania?
faq.a: A commissioned inspector, working with the repair organization that holds a National Board R stamp. The Department of Labor and Industry Boiler Division regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels in the state.

faq.q: Why are penetrant materials lot-controlled for stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Halogens and sulfur in penetrant residues can cause cracking or attack on those alloys in service. Lot-certified materials with low content are used and documented in the job file.

faq.q: Can Atlantis teach my staff penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A and a penetrant simulator. Your employer certifies personnel under its own written practice.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing Philadelphia, PA: What Atlantis Offers
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. Philadelphia, PA buyers can get UT as a volumetric alternative and Level III radiograph review.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Support in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
rt.html:
Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, including Philadelphia. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission sets the federal rules in 10 CFR Part 34, and Pennsylvania, an Agreement State, administers equivalent radiation protection rules through its own state program. Atlantis holds no source license and does not offer to expose or interpret film as a radiography contractor. This page explains what we can do for a Philadelphia owner who searched for RT.

Why radiography is not part of our Philadelphia services

Radiography requires sealed gamma sources or X-ray equipment, trained and licensed radiographers, security for the source, controlled exclusion areas and a radiation safety program. Those obligations sit with the licensee. A company without that license cannot lawfully provide the service, and Atlantis chooses not to claim it. If your contract requires radiography, the owner or engineer should select a licensed contractor against the specification and verify the license before mobilization.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative in Philadelphia

Where the construction code and the owner permit, ultrasonic examination can stand in for radiography when the question is weld volume. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 provide for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 sets ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows it in place of radiography only under specific conditions. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector, before the job starts.

When that agreement is in place, Level II technicians travel to your site and perform shear wave examination to a procedure approved by an ASNT Level III. Read about ultrasonic testing in Philadelphia and our national UT service. Surface checks on the same weld are available through magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing, and the state hub, NDT inspection services in Pennsylvania, lists wider coverage.

Level III review of radiographs and RT documents

Review work uses no radioactive source and needs no radiation license. Atlantis founder Anoop Rayavarapu is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and can support Philadelphia owners with:

  • Independent review of radiographs, in film or image form, and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.
  • A second opinion on any indication the owner and the contractor read differently, before a weld is cut out or accepted.
  • Review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice before the work begins.

Send the images and the governing code through this radiograph review request and we reply within one business day. For program help, see Level III consulting and written practice development.

Radiography theory training

Teams who need to understand radiography can study the principles, image quality and interpretation in our RT Level 2 course. The course does not license anyone to operate sources, and certification remains with the employer under its written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A.

Planning with Atlantis in Philadelphia

Atlantis keeps no office in Philadelphia. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city for inspection scopes, and radiograph review is done remotely from the images you send. Share the metal, wall thickness, governing code and the radiography clause in your contract, and the reply will state plainly which parts fall inside our scope.

faq.q: Why does Atlantis not perform radiographic testing in Philadelphia?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because it is licensed under NRC rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or equivalent Agreement State rules, and we do not offer it.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Philadelphia weld?
faq.a: In some cases. Pipeline, process piping and structural codes each set their own ultrasonic provisions, and pressure vessel rules allow the swap only under defined conditions, so agree it with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can an ASNT Level III review radiographs made by someone else?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III can review radiographs and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and provide a second read on disputed indications. No radiation license is needed for review.

faq.q: Do you teach radiography?
faq.a: The RT Level 2 course covers theory only: image quality, exposure principles and interpretation. Completing it does not authorize anyone to run sources, and qualification still comes from the employer.

faq.q: How do I ask for a radiograph review in Philadelphia?
faq.a: Use the review request link on this page, attach images or describe the code and weld, and we reply within one business day with whether the review fits our scope.
